title.text: More ways to lose a license

why_how.text: Colorado links the driving privilege to legal duties beyond driving, such as paying child support and carrying insurance.
An under-twenty-one alcohol purchase or possession conviction can cost the privilege because the state treats underage drinking seriously.

scenario.text: Jordan, nineteen, is convicted of buying beer but was never behind the wheel that night.

reasoning.text: The ground is the under-twenty-one alcohol conviction itself, not any driving.

result.text: Jordan's driving privilege can be lost even though no driving was involved.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing a license can only be lost for something you did while driving.

correction.text: Unpaid court-ordered child support and an under-twenty-one alcohol conviction can each cost the privilege without any driving.

prompt.text: An officer asks a driver for proof of insurance and the driver has none. What is at risk?

rationale.text: You must carry proof of insurance whenever you drive, and failing to show it can cost your license.

lines.text: Some grounds have nothing to do with the road.

narration.text: In the last chapter you met the main reasons a Colorado license can be suspended, revoked or canceled. This lesson adds three more, and they surprise many people because none of them requires a dangerous move on the road. One is about family court, one is about paperwork you carry in the car, and one is about young people and alcohol. Learning them now helps you see the driving privilege the way the state does: as something tied to meeting your legal responsibilities, not only to how well you steer and brake. Each one shows up in practice questions.

lines.text: No proof of insurance when asked.

narration.text: First, failing to pay court-ordered child support is another way to lose your Colorado driving privilege. The state can use the license as leverage to get support paid. Second, you must carry proof of insurance whenever you drive. If an officer asks and you cannot show valid evidence of insurance, that failure can cost you your license. Notice the wording: carrying the proof is the duty. Having a policy at home in a drawer does not help during a traffic stop. Keep a current insurance card in the vehicle, or have valid proof ready to show whenever you drive.

lines.text: Buying or possessing alcohol under twenty-one.

narration.text: Third, a conviction for buying or possessing alcohol while under twenty-one can also lead to losing your driving privilege. This rule is about the conviction, not about a car. A teenager caught buying beer at a store or holding a drink at a party can face it even if they walked there. The state ties underage alcohol to the license because the license is a strong motivator for young people. Later in this chapter you will see that the same idea appears in the rules for drivers under twenty-one, where possession alone can lead to revocation without any driving involved.

lines.text: Losing a license can happen off the road.
Child support and alcohol cases count.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many people believe a license can only be lost for something done while driving, like speeding or impaired driving. That is not true in Colorado. Unpaid court-ordered child support can cost the privilege. An under-twenty-one conviction for buying or possessing alcohol can cost it too, even with no driving at all. And the insurance rule, while it involves a traffic stop, is about proof you carry rather than how you drove. When a practice question describes a person who never drove badly but has one of these problems, the license is still at risk.

Here is a quick check: an officer pulls over a driver for a broken tail light and asks for proof of insurance. The driver says the policy is paid up, but has no card or other proof to show. What is at risk? Think about the rule before reading on. The driver's license is at risk. Colorado requires you to carry proof of insurance whenever you drive, and failing to show valid evidence when an officer asks can cost you your license. The duty is not only to be insured, but to be able to prove it on the spot. Keep valid proof in the vehicle every time you drive.

Let us wrap up. Three more grounds can cost your Colorado driving privilege. Failing to pay court-ordered child support is one. Failing to show valid proof of insurance when an officer asks is another, so always carry proof whenever you drive. A conviction for buying or possessing alcohol while under twenty-one is the third, and it applies even when no driving was involved. Together with points, impaired driving, refusal and crash conduct, these complete a picture of the license as a privilege tied to responsibility. Next, we turn to seat belts and who must wear them.

why_how.text: Seat belts are required for those most at risk in a crash: the driver, front-seat riders and children.
Exceptions are kept narrow so the rule protects almost everyone in the car.

scenario.text: Taylor, seventeen, drives three friends in a car with five seat belts.

reasoning.text: Because the driver is under eighteen, every passenger must be belted and the passengers may not outnumber the belts.

result.text: All three friends buckle up, front and back, and no one rides without a belt.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking delivery-van drivers never have to wear a seat belt.

correction.text: Delivery-van drivers are exempt only while on the job; off duty, the seat belt rule applies.

prompt.text: A delivery-van driver uses the van for a weekend trip. Is the driver exempt from the seat belt rule?

answer.text: No. The exemption covers delivery-van drivers only while they are working.

rationale.text: The exception is tied to the job, not to the vehicle.

narration.text: Seat belts save lives, and Colorado spells out exactly who must wear one. This lesson covers three things: who the basic rule protects, the short list of exceptions, and the stricter rule when the person behind the wheel is under eighteen. Exam questions in this area often hinge on one detail, such as which seat a passenger is in, how old a child is, or whether a worker is on the job. So as we go, pay attention to the conditions attached to each rule, because those conditions are what separate a right answer from a tempting wrong one.

On public roads, Colorado requires a fastened seat belt in every vehicle with factory-installed belts for the driver, every front-seat passenger, and every child under sixteen. Read that list carefully. The driver and the front seat are always covered. In the back seat, children under sixteen are covered too. A child's age, not just the seat they sit in, decides whether the rule reaches them in the back. The phrase factory-installed belts matters as well: the rule applies to vehicles built with belts. When a question asks who must buckle, check the seat and the age.

lines.text: Passenger and school buses, farm equipment.

narration.text: The exceptions are few, and the handbook calls them the only ones. Emergency personnel are exempt. So are passenger and school buses, and farm equipment. Delivery-van drivers are exempt while they are working. And anyone carrying a physician statement saying they cannot wear a belt for physical or psychological reasons is exempt. Notice what is not on the list: short trips, slow speeds, discomfort, or sitting in the back as an adult passenger in someone else's car when the driver is an adult. If a reason is not on this list, it is not an exception, however reasonable it sounds.

Here is the trap hidden in the exceptions. Delivery-van drivers are exempt only while on the job. People often remember the delivery-van exemption but forget the limit, and assume anyone in a delivery van never has to buckle. That is not the rule. The same driver, in the same van, on a personal errand after work, must wear a seat belt like anyone else. The exemption follows the work, not the vehicle. When a practice question describes a delivery driver, look for whether they are working at that moment before deciding whether the seat belt rule applies to them.

title.text: When the driver is a teen

lines.text: Driver under eighteen: every passenger belted.
No more passengers than seat belts.

narration.text: The rule tightens when the driver is under eighteen. In that case, every passenger must be belted or properly restrained, no matter where they sit or how old they are. And the passenger count may never be more than the number of seat belts. So a teen driver cannot squeeze an extra friend into a car whose belts are already in use, even for a short ride. This works alongside the passenger limits you learned for new minor drivers. Both rules point the same way: a young driver's car carries only as many people as it can safely restrain.

lines.text: A delivery van on a weekend trip.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a delivery-van driver borrows the work van for a weekend trip to visit family. Does the delivery-van exemption from the seat belt rule still apply? Think about the condition attached to the exemption before reading the answer. It does not apply. Delivery-van drivers are exempt only while they are working. On a personal trip, the driver must wear a seat belt like any other driver. The handbook lists only a few exceptions, and each one has its own condition. Here, the condition is being on the job, and a weekend family visit does not meet it.

lines.text: Driver, front seat, children under sixteen.
Few exceptions, each with a condition.

narration.text: Let us review. In vehicles with factory-installed belts on Colorado public roads, the driver, every front-seat passenger and every child under sixteen must wear a fastened seat belt. The only exceptions are emergency personnel, passenger and school buses, farm equipment, delivery-van drivers while working, and people with a physician statement. When the driver is under eighteen, every passenger must be belted or properly restrained, and passengers may never outnumber the seat belts. Next, we look at how to restrain young children, which depends on their age and weight.

why_how.text: Young children need restraints matched to their size, because an adult belt does not fit a small body safely.
The driver must check each child's restraint when no parent is in the car, so the responsibility never falls through the cracks.

scenario.text: You are driving a neighbor's two children: an eighteen-month-old who weighs twenty-two pounds and a five-year-old who weighs forty-four pounds.

reasoning.text: The toddler is under two and under forty pounds, so rear-facing in back; the five-year-old is in the four to under nine band at forty pounds or more.

result.text: The toddler rides rear-facing in the back seat, and the five-year-old uses a child restraint or booster in the back seat.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every child under two must always ride rear-facing.

correction.text: A child under two who weighs forty pounds or more may ride rear-facing or forward-facing.

prompt.text: A child under two weighs forty-two pounds. Which directions of child restraint are allowed?

rationale.text: Under forty pounds means rear-facing in back; at forty pounds or more, either direction is allowed.

narration.text: Child restraint rules can look like a wall of numbers, but they follow a simple idea: match the restraint to the child's age and weight. This lesson begins with who is responsible when no parent is in the car, then walks up through each age band, from children younger than two to teenagers up to eighteen. Along the way we will highlight the two weight lines that cause the most confusion. If you learn the bands in order, each one becomes easier to remember, because each step up gives an older, heavier child a little more flexibility in how they ride.

Start with responsibility. When no parent is in the vehicle, the driver is responsible for making sure each child is properly secured in the correct child restraint. That covers grandparents, babysitters, older siblings, carpool drivers and anyone else giving a child a ride. It does not matter whose car it is or how short the trip will be. The driver checks that each child has the right kind of restraint for their age and weight and that it is used correctly. This is why the age and weight bands in the rest of this lesson matter to every driver, not only to parents.

lines.text: Under forty pounds: rear-facing, back seat.
Forty pounds or more: either direction.

narration.text: For children younger than two, weight decides the rule. A child younger than two who weighs less than forty pounds must ride in a rear-facing child restraint in the back seat. A child younger than two who weighs forty pounds or more may ride in either a rear-facing or a forward-facing child restraint. Most very young children fall under the forty-pound line, so rear-facing in the back seat is the usual answer. But do not overlook the heavier child. When a practice question gives you a child under two, look at the weight before choosing between rear-facing only and either direction.

lines.text: Under two is not always rear-facing.
Forty pounds is the dividing line.

narration.text: Here is the first trap. Many people remember that babies ride rear-facing and stop there. But the rule for a child under two turns on weight. Under forty pounds means rear-facing in the back seat. Forty pounds or more allows rear-facing or forward-facing. So an answer that says every child under two must always face the rear is too strict. And an answer that lets a twenty-five-pound one-year-old face forward is too loose. The fix is to treat forty pounds as the switch inside the under-two band, and to read the child's weight before the child's age settles your answer.

lines.text: Two to under four, at least twenty pounds.
Four to under nine, at least forty pounds.

narration.text: Next come two bands with their own weight minimums. A child aged two to under four who weighs at least twenty pounds must ride in a rear-facing or forward-facing child restraint, in the back seat when one is available. A child aged four to under nine who weighs at least forty pounds must use a child restraint or booster seat in the back seat when the vehicle has one. Notice the booster seat appears only in the older band. Notice also that both rules prefer the back seat whenever the vehicle has one, which keeps young children away from the front of the car.

lines.text: Twenty pounds: ages two to under four.
Forty pounds: ages four to under nine.

narration.text: Here is the second trap. Two different weight minimums sit side by side. The twenty-pound minimum belongs to the age two to under four band. The forty-pound minimum belongs to the age four to under nine band, the one that allows a booster seat. Questions swap these numbers to see whether you have attached each one to the right age. A helpful way to hold them is that the smaller number goes with the younger children. And remember that forty pounds also appears in the under-two band, where it splits rear-facing from either direction, so always pair the weight with the age.

Here is a quick check: you are driving a child who is twenty months old and weighs forty-two pounds. No parent is in the car. Which directions of child restraint are allowed, and who must check it? Decide before reading on. Either a rear-facing or a forward-facing child restraint is allowed, because a child younger than two who weighs forty pounds or more may use either. If the same child weighed thirty pounds, the answer would be rear-facing in the back seat only. And because no parent is present, you, the driver, are responsible for making sure the child is properly secured.

lines.text: Driver checks when no parent rides.
Nine to eighteen: belt or restraint.

narration.text: Let us pull it together. With no parent in the vehicle, the driver makes sure every child is properly restrained. Under two and under forty pounds rides rear-facing in the back seat; under two and forty pounds or more may face either way. Ages two to under four, at least twenty pounds, use a rear-facing or forward-facing restraint, in back when available. Ages four to under nine, at least forty pounds, use a child restraint or booster in back when the vehicle has one. Children from nine to eighteen use a seat belt or a child restraint as the manufacturer directs.

why_how.text: Alcohol is a depressant, so it slows the reactions and judgment that safe driving depends on.
Because BAC depends on personal factors and only time lowers it, guessing your own safety after drinking is unreliable.

scenario.text: After a party, Alex switches from shots of whiskey to beer and then drinks two cups of coffee before leaving.

reasoning.text: Each standard drink holds about the same alcohol, and coffee does not lower BAC; only time does.

result.text: Alex's BAC has not been lowered by the beer or the coffee, so Alex should not drive.

claim.text: Many people think coffee, a cold shower or fresh air can sober you up faster.

correction.text: BAC drops only with time, at about zero point zero one five percent per hour on average; nothing else speeds it up.

memory_support.text: A drink is a drink; only time works.

prompt.text: A driver switches from wine to beer, thinking it will keep BAC lower. Does it?

answer.text: No. Each standard drink of beer, wine or spirits holds about the same alcohol.

rationale.text: Switching drink types does not make you safer, because a standard drink is the same alcohol whatever it is.

narration.text: This lesson is about what alcohol actually does to a driver, and about the myths that lead people to drive when they should not. Impaired driving is among the leading causes of crashes and deaths on the road, so these facts matter well beyond the test. You will learn how alcohol affects the brain and body, what the open container rule covers, what determines a person's blood alcohol concentration, why every standard drink counts the same, and why only time can bring your BAC down. Each of these facts takes apart a common belief that people use to talk themselves into driving.

lines.text: Among the leading causes of deaths.

narration.text: Impaired driving by alcohol, drugs or a mix of them is among the leading causes of crashes and deaths on the road. Alcohol is a depressant. It slows brain function, reflexes and reaction time. It harms thinking and coordination, which are the skills you use to judge gaps, speeds and distances. It also makes risky moves such as speeding or abrupt turns more likely, because it lowers the caution that normally holds those choices back. So a drinking driver is hit twice: slower to react to danger, and more likely to create it. That combination is why impaired driving is treated so seriously.

lines.text: No open alcohol in the passenger area.

narration.text: Colorado also controls what you carry. It is illegal to have an open container of alcohol or of marijuana in the passenger area of a vehicle on a public road. This applies to the whole passenger area, not just the driver's hand, and it applies to marijuana as well as alcohol. The rule removes the temptation and the evidence problem at the same time: if nothing is open inside the passenger area, no one is drinking or using while the car is moving. A sealed container stored outside the passenger area is a different situation from an open one sitting in a cup holder.

lines.text: How much and how fast you drank.

narration.text: Your blood alcohol concentration, or BAC, depends on how much you drank, your body weight, how fast you drank, how long it has been since your last drink, and your sex. That is why two people drinking the same amount can end up with different BAC levels. A smaller person who drank quickly may be far more impaired than a larger friend who drank slowly over the evening. This makes it unreliable to judge your own safety by comparing yourself to someone else, or by counting drinks without considering the other factors. The safest plan is not to drive after drinking at all.

lines.text: One and a half ounces of spirits.

narration.text: Here is a common myth: that beer or wine is safer than hard liquor. Per standard drink, beer, wine and liquor are equally intoxicating. Twelve ounces of beer, five ounces of wine and one and a half ounces of distilled spirits each hold about the same amount of alcohol. So switching from whiskey to beer does not make you safer; it only changes the glass. When a practice question suggests a driver stayed safe by sticking to beer, the answer is that each standard drink still added the same alcohol. Count drinks, not drink types.

lines.text: Showers and fresh air do not help.
About zero point zero one five percent per hour.

narration.text: Here is the second myth: that coffee, a cold shower or fresh air can sober you up. Only time sobers you up. On average, BAC falls by about zero point zero one five percent per hour, and nothing else speeds it up. Coffee may make a person feel more awake, but their BAC is unchanged, and so is their impairment. That gap between feeling alert and being sober is exactly what makes these myths dangerous. If you have been drinking, the only fix is to wait long enough, and the simplest way to stay safe is to arrange another way home.

Here is a quick check: at a wedding, a guest drinks two glasses of wine and then switches to beer, believing beer will keep their BAC lower so they can drive home. Is that belief correct? Answer before reading on. It is not. Per standard drink, beer, wine and liquor hold about the same alcohol, so switching drink types does not make anyone safer. Their BAC depends on how much they drank, how fast, their body weight, their sex and the time since their last drink. And only time will lower it, so the guest should not drive.

lines.text: Alcohol slows you and raises risk.

narration.text: Let us review. Impaired driving is among the leading causes of crashes and deaths. Alcohol is a depressant that slows brain function, reflexes and reaction time, harms thinking and coordination, and makes risky moves more likely. Open containers of alcohol or marijuana are illegal in the passenger area on a public road. BAC depends on amount, body weight, speed of drinking, time since the last drink and sex. A standard drink of beer, wine or spirits holds about the same alcohol. Only time sobers you up, at about zero point zero one five percent per hour. Next come the impaired-driving charges.

why_how.text: Colorado separates slight impairment from substantial impairment so the charge fits how impaired the driver was.
A conviction can rest on behavior and observations, so a driver below a BAC line can still be charged.

scenario.text: A driver weaves slightly, fumbles field sobriety tests, and refuses a chemical test.

reasoning.text: Impairment can be proven by behavior, observations and field sobriety tests, and refusing a chemical test is its own ground for revocation.

result.text: The driver can face an impaired-driving charge and license revocation without any BAC number.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking DWAI and DUI are just two names for the same charge.

correction.text: DWAI means impaired to the slightest degree, DUI means substantially incapable of driving safely, and DUI per se is set by BAC.

memory_support.text: Slight, substantial, or by the number.

prompt.text: A driver is impaired only slightly. Which charge fits?

rationale.text: DWAI covers impairment to even the slightest degree; DUI requires being substantially incapable of driving safely.

narration.text: Colorado uses more than one impaired-driving charge, and the differences show up often in practice questions. This lesson explains what DWAI and DUI each mean, what DUI per se adds, how an impaired-driving case can be proven even without a BAC number, and the BAC levels that can lead to license revocation for different kinds of drivers. By the end, you should be able to read a short scenario and decide which charge fits and which BAC line applies. Keep in mind that the charges describe degrees of impairment, while the BAC lines describe measured numbers.

lines.text: DWAI: impaired to the slightest degree.
DUI: substantially incapable of driving safely.

narration.text: DWAI stands for Driving While Ability Impaired. It means impairment to even the slightest degree. DUI stands for Driving Under the Influence. It means being substantially incapable of driving safely. So the difference is one of degree. A driver whose abilities are dulled only a little can still be charged with DWAI. A driver who is substantially unable to drive safely faces DUI. Neither charge requires a crash. Both cover impairment by alcohol, drugs or a combination. When a question describes how impaired someone was, match slight to DWAI and substantial to DUI.

lines.text: BAC greater than zero point zero eight percent.

narration.text: DUI per se adds a measured line. A driver can be convicted of DUI per se when BAC is greater than zero point zero eight percent. Per se means by itself: the BAC number alone is enough for this charge, whatever the driver's behavior looked like. So there are really three ideas here. DWAI is slight impairment. DUI is substantial impairment. DUI per se is a BAC above zero point zero eight percent. A driver could be well-spoken and steady on their feet and still face DUI per se if the measured BAC is over the line. Keep the three ideas separate as you study.

lines.text: BAC over the line: DUI per se.

narration.text: Here is the trap: treating DWAI and DUI as the same thing, or assuming every charge depends on a BAC number. DWAI means impaired even slightly. DUI means substantially unable to drive safely. DUI per se is based on BAC above zero point zero eight percent. Questions often describe a driver with a modest BAC who was still clearly affected, and the tempting wrong answer says no charge is possible. But DWAI reaches even slight impairment. Other questions describe a high BAC with no visible signs, and the wrong answer says the driver is fine. DUI per se covers that.

An impaired-driving conviction does not rest on BAC alone. It can be proven by driving behavior, the officer's observations during the stop, and performance on Standardized Field Sobriety Tests. So weaving, slurred speech or failing the field tests can all become evidence. Separately, your license may be revoked for refusing a chemical test, or for a BAC over the revocation line that applies to you. Refusing a test does not make the case go away; it creates its own ground for revocation. The safest conclusion is simple: there is no technical way to drink and drive safely.

The BAC level that can lead to revocation depends on who is driving. Most adults have one line, drivers under twenty-one have a much lower line, and drivers with a commercial driver license, or CDL, have a line in between. The handbook lists all three next to the refusal rule, so the same paragraph covers refusing a test and exceeding your line. When a practice question names a young driver or a commercial driver, do not apply the general adult line. Drivers under twenty-one face the strictest limit of all, which fits the state's approach to young people and alcohol.

Here is a quick check: after two drinks, a driver is only slightly affected, but an officer notices slow reactions and a poor field sobriety test. Which impaired-driving charge fits this level of impairment? Decide first. DWAI, Driving While Ability Impaired, fits, because it covers impairment to even the slightest degree. DUI would require being substantially incapable of driving safely. And remember that the case does not need a BAC number: driving behavior, officer observations and field sobriety tests can all prove impairment. If the driver refused a chemical test, that refusal could also lead to revocation.

lines.text: Per se above the BAC line.
Lower lines for young and CDL drivers.

narration.text: Let us review. DWAI means impairment to even the slightest degree, and DUI means being substantially incapable of driving safely. DUI per se applies when BAC is greater than zero point zero eight percent. An impaired-driving case can be proven by driving behavior, officer observations and field sobriety tests, not only by BAC. Your license may be revoked for refusing a chemical test or for a BAC over the line that applies to you, and that line is lower for drivers under twenty-one and for CDL drivers. Next, we look at the penalties for each conviction.

why_how.text: Penalties rise with each repeat conviction to discourage drivers from impaired driving again.
A first DWAI is handled with points, while a first DUI goes straight to revocation, reflecting the difference in impairment.

scenario.text: Chris, twenty-five, has one prior DUI and is convicted of DWAI.

reasoning.text: A second DWAI or DUI brings a one-year revocation, with a fine, jail time and public service.

result.text: Chris faces a one-year revocation, not eight points, because this is a second conviction.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a first DUI, like a first DWAI, is handled with points.

correction.text: Only the first DWAI is measured in points, eight of them; a first DUI brings a nine-month revocation instead.

memory_support.text: Points first, then nine, twelve, twenty-four months.

prompt.text: A twenty-two-year-old is convicted of a first DUI. What revocation applies?

rationale.text: A first DUI brings a nine-month revocation, while a first DWAI is the one measured in points.

narration.text: This lesson lays out the penalties for impaired-driving convictions for drivers twenty-one or older. Rather than memorizing every fine and jail range, focus on the shape of the system. A first DWAI is the one conviction measured in points. A first DUI brings a revocation instead. Then, with each repeat conviction, the revocation grows longer. Fines, jail time and public service hours come with every level too, and they generally climb as well. If you can place a conviction on that ladder, you can answer most penalty questions, even when the specific dollar figures blur together.

lines.text: Tied to a zero point zero five percent BAC level.

narration.text: A first DWAI conviction for a driver twenty-one or older is tied to a zero point zero five percent BAC level. It carries eight points, a fine of two hundred to five hundred dollars, two to one hundred eighty days in jail, and twenty-four to forty-eight hours of public service. The eight points are the feature to remember. Of all the listed impaired-driving convictions, this is the only one measured in points rather than a revocation. That does not make it minor: eight points is a large share of what it takes to lose a license, and the fine, jail and service are real.

lines.text: Tied to zero point zero eight percent BAC.

narration.text: A first DUI for a driver twenty-one or older is tied to a zero point zero eight percent BAC and brings a nine-month revocation. It also brings a fine of six hundred to one thousand dollars, five to three hundred sixty-five days in jail, and forty-eight to ninety-six hours of public service. Compared with a first DWAI, every part is heavier, and the license itself is revoked rather than charged with points. That jump reflects the difference between slight impairment and being substantially incapable of driving safely. If a question says first DUI, think nine months without a license.

Here is the trap. Because a first DWAI is measured in points, people sometimes assume a first DUI works the same way. It does not. The first DWAI is the only listed impaired-driving conviction measured in points, eight of them. A first DUI brings a nine-month revocation instead. So when a practice question offers eight points as the result of a first DUI, that is the DWAI penalty borrowed into the wrong row. And when it offers a revocation for a first DWAI, that borrows from the DUI row. Keep the first conviction of each charge in its own lane.

lines.text: Larger fines and longer jail ranges.

narration.text: Repeat convictions are handled more harshly. A second DWAI or DUI brings a one-year revocation, a fine of six hundred to fifteen hundred dollars, ten to three hundred sixty-five days in jail, and forty-eight to one hundred twenty hours of public service. A third or later DWAI or DUI brings a two-year revocation, the same fine range, sixty to three hundred sixty-five days in jail, and the same public service range. Notice that from the second conviction on, DWAI and DUI are treated together. What matters at that point is how many convictions the driver already has.

lines.text: Nine months for a first DUI.
Two years for a third or later.

narration.text: Here is the second trap, about the ladder itself. Revocation length climbs with repeat convictions: nine months for a first DUI, one year for a second DWAI or DUI, and two years for a third or later. Questions often swap two of these rungs, offering one year for a first DUI or nine months for a second. A quick way to check yourself is that the numbers only go up. Nine months, then twelve, then twenty-four. If an answer makes the penalty shrink or stay flat as convictions add up, it cannot be right. Count prior convictions first, then climb the ladder.

Here is a quick check: a twenty-two-year-old with no prior record is convicted of a first DUI. What revocation applies, and how would the answer change if the conviction were a first DWAI instead? Work it out before reading on. A first DUI brings a nine-month revocation, along with a fine, possible jail time and public service. A first DWAI would not bring a revocation; it is the only listed conviction measured in points, eight of them. If the same driver were later convicted again, the revocation would climb to one year, and a third would bring two years.

Let us review the ladder for drivers twenty-one or older. A first DWAI, tied to a zero point zero five percent BAC level, carries eight points along with a fine, jail and public service. A first DUI, tied to zero point zero eight percent, brings a nine-month revocation and heavier fines, jail and service. A second DWAI or DUI brings a one-year revocation, and a third or later brings two years, each with fines, jail and public service. The first DWAI is the only one measured in points. Next, we look at the special rules for drivers under twenty-one.

why_how.text: Colorado gives young drivers a chance to complete a court-ordered program after a first conviction, but not after repeats.
Alcohol possession can cost a young person's license because the privilege is a strong incentive to stay away from alcohol.

scenario.text: Sam, twenty, is convicted of a first DWAI and is ordered to complete an evaluation and program.

reasoning.text: For a first conviction under twenty-one, revocation follows if the court-ordered evaluation or program is not finished.

result.text: Sam finishes the program, which avoids the first-conviction revocation; a second conviction would mean mandatory revocation.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a young person's license can only be revoked for something done while driving.

correction.text: Anyone under twenty-one convicted of buying or possessing alcohol can have their privilege revoked even with no driving.

memory_support.text: Finish the program, or lose it.

prompt.text: A twenty-year-old has a second impaired-driving conviction. What happens to the license?

answer.text: It is revoked; a second or third conviction means mandatory revocation.

rationale.text: Only a first conviction depends on finishing the court-ordered program.

narration.text: Drivers under twenty-one face their own set of alcohol rules in Colorado. You already know that their BAC revocation line is the lowest of all. This lesson adds what happens after a conviction. A first impaired-driving conviction comes with a chance to avoid revocation by completing a court-ordered program, while repeat convictions bring mandatory revocation. And separately, a young person can lose the privilege for buying or possessing alcohol even if they never drove. Pay attention to whether a scenario describes a first conviction or a repeat, and whether any driving happened at all.

lines.text: First: revoked if the program is not finished.

narration.text: A driver under twenty-one convicted of DUI or DWAI faces revocation on a first conviction if they do not finish the court-ordered evaluation or program. Finishing the evaluation or program is what keeps that first conviction from leading to revocation. A second or third conviction means mandatory revocation, with no program option to avoid it. So the system gives a young driver one chance to respond, and then removes the choice. When a question asks about an under-twenty-one driver, the first thing to find is how many impaired-driving convictions they have, then whether any program was finished.

lines.text: Buying or possessing alcohol under twenty-one.

narration.text: The second rule does not involve a car at all. Anyone under twenty-one convicted of buying or possessing alcohol can have their driving privilege revoked even when no driving was involved. So a nineteen-year-old caught with a beer at a park, who walked there, can still lose their license. This matches what you learned at the start of the chapter, where an under-twenty-one alcohol conviction was listed among the ways to lose the privilege. The license is used as an incentive. For young people, staying away from alcohol protects their ability to drive, whether or not they were behind the wheel.

Here is the trap. For drivers under twenty-one, a first DUI or DWAI leads to revocation only if the court-ordered evaluation or program is not completed. But a second or third conviction is always revoked. Questions blur these two in both directions. One wrong answer says a young driver is always revoked on a first conviction, ignoring the program. Another says finishing a program after a second conviction saves the license, borrowing the first-conviction rule. Keep them apart: the program matters only for the first conviction. After that, revocation is mandatory, regardless of programs.

Here is a quick check: a twenty-year-old who completed a court-ordered program after a first DWAI is now convicted of a second DWAI. The driver says finishing the program last time should protect the license again. Is that right? Think before reading on. It is not. For drivers under twenty-one, only a first conviction depends on finishing the court-ordered evaluation or program. A second or third conviction means mandatory revocation. And remember that separate rule: buying or possessing alcohol under twenty-one can cost the license even without any driving.

Let us wrap up. A driver under twenty-one convicted of a first DUI or DWAI faces revocation if they do not finish the court-ordered evaluation or program. A second or third conviction means mandatory revocation. Separately, anyone under twenty-one convicted of buying or possessing alcohol can have their driving privilege revoked, even when no driving was involved. Combined with the lowest BAC revocation line, these rules make alcohol especially costly for young drivers. Next, we turn from alcohol to drugs, including medicines, and how they are treated behind the wheel.

why_how.text: Any drug that impairs you makes driving dangerous, so Colorado penalizes drug impairment just like alcohol impairment.
Medicines affect people differently, which is why labels and a pharmacist's advice matter before driving.

scenario.text: Morgan takes an over-the-counter cold remedy that makes them drowsy, then plans to drive to work.

reasoning.text: Cold remedies can impair driving, and driving impaired by any drug carries the same penalties as alcohol.

result.text: Morgan reads the label, sees a drowsiness warning, and arranges another ride.

claim.text: Many people think a legal prescription or a medical marijuana card makes impaired driving acceptable.

correction.text: Legal or medical use does not excuse impaired driving; it is penalized like alcohol impairment.

prompt.text: A driver with a medical marijuana card is impaired and charged with DWAI. Is the card a defense?

answer.text: No. Medical use is no defense to a DUI or DWAI charge.

rationale.text: Legal or medical use does not excuse impaired driving; the penalties match alcohol impairment.

narration.text: Alcohol is not the only substance that impairs drivers. This lesson covers drugs of every kind, from illegal drugs and marijuana to prescription and over-the-counter medicines. You will learn how Colorado treats drug-impaired driving, why a medical reason does not work as a defense, which everyday medicines can affect your driving, and what to do before you drive after taking one. The theme is simple: the law cares about whether you are impaired, not about whether the substance was legal to buy or prescribed by a doctor. That idea runs through every question in this area.

Driving impaired by any drug, whether illegal drugs, marijuana, prescription or over-the-counter medicine, is illegal and carries the same penalties as alcohol-impaired driving. So everything you learned about DWAI, DUI and the penalty ladder applies here too. A driver impaired by a prescription painkiller faces the same kind of charge as a driver impaired by alcohol. The question is never whether the drug itself was legal. It is whether the driver was impaired. That is why the handbook places drugs right alongside alcohol rather than in a separate, gentler category.

lines.text: Neither is any medical drug use.

narration.text: Using marijuana or another drug for medical reasons is no defense to a DUI or DWAI charge. A medical marijuana card or a valid prescription may make it legal to possess and use the drug, but it does not make it legal to drive while impaired by it. People sometimes treat the card or prescription as permission to drive however they feel, and that is exactly the misunderstanding the handbook addresses. If a medicine affects your ability to drive safely, the medical reason for taking it does not change the outcome of an impaired-driving charge.

Here is the trap. Many people think that if a drug is legal for them, driving after using it must be legal too. Not in Colorado. Legal or medical use of a drug does not excuse impaired driving. Prescription, over-the-counter and medical marijuana impairment are all penalized like alcohol. So a practice question may describe a driver with a valid prescription who drove impaired and offer an answer saying no charge applies. That answer is wrong. Separate the two questions in your head: is the drug legal to use, and is the driver impaired? Only the second decides the charge.

lines.text: Effects depend on dose and person.

narration.text: Drug impairment depends on the dose and the person. Tranquilizers, pain killers and allergy or cold remedies can all impair driving, even when taken as directed. Because effects vary, read medication labels for warnings before you drive. When a label is missing or unclear, ask your doctor or pharmacist. This is practical advice as much as a rule. A sniffle remedy taken before a commute can cause drowsiness that is just as dangerous as a drink, and the law treats the resulting impairment the same way. A short check before you drive can prevent a long problem afterward.

Here is a quick check: a driver who holds a medical marijuana card uses marijuana, drives while impaired, and is charged with DWAI. In court, the driver argues that the medical card is a defense. Will that argument work? Answer before reading on. It will not. Using marijuana or another drug for medical reasons is no defense to a DUI or DWAI charge. Legal or medical use does not excuse impaired driving, and drug impairment is penalized just like alcohol impairment. The card may make use legal, but it never makes impaired driving legal.

Let us close the chapter. Driving impaired by any drug, including illegal drugs, marijuana, prescription and over-the-counter medicine, is illegal and carries the same penalties as alcohol-impaired driving. Medical use of marijuana or another drug is no defense to a DUI or DWAI charge. Drug effects depend on the dose and the person, and tranquilizers, pain killers and allergy or cold remedies can all impair driving. Read medication labels before you drive, and ask your doctor or pharmacist when a label is missing or unclear. The rule throughout is the same: impairment, not legality, decides.
